description: Capsule is a Walrus native marketplace for verifiable private knowledge. It enables publishers to monetise selected fragments of private datasets, research reports, diligence documents, market intelligence, and AI evaluation data without exposing the complete source. Today, when someone purchases an excerpt from a private document, they must trust that the seller has delivered authentic content. The excerpt could be modified, fabricated, or copied from another source, and the buyer has no independent way to verify it. Capsule replaces this trust with cryptographic proof. A publisher uploads a line oriented document through the Capsule interface and defines fixed sections that can be purchased independently. Inside the publisher’s browser, Capsule constructs a salted SHA-256 Merkle tree, generates inclusion proofs, and encrypts every sellable fragment using Seal before any private content leaves the device. The disclosure host receives only ciphertext and public metadata, never the complete plaintext document or a reusable source encryption key. The encrypted fragments and document manifest are stored durably on Walrus. Capsule then registers the document commitment, fragment ranges, Walrus references, pricing, and Seal identities through its Sui Move contract. Walrus serves as the permanent encrypted artifact layer, while Sui provides the public coordination and provenance layer. A buyer connects a Sui wallet, selects the exact fragment they need, and signs an on-chain purchase_fragment transaction. The Move contract validates the exact payment, transfers SUI to the publisher, and creates a public Purchase object bound to the buyer, document, and specific encrypted fragment. This is a real onchain purchase receipt, not merely a marketplace database entry. After validating the purchase, Capsule creates an encrypted delivery wrapper, stores it on Walrus, and records a Disclosure object on Sui. The buyer then authorises a short lived Seal session. Capsule’s Move access policy verifies that the requesting wallet is the recorded buyer and that the purchase is bound to the correct document, fragment, range, and Seal identity. Only then does Seal permit local decryption. Once decrypted, the buyer’s browser verifies the fragment independently. It recomputes the Merkle root from the disclosed lines, salts, and proof path, then compares the result with the public root stored on Sui. The buyer therefore does not need to trust Capsule, the publisher, or the disclosure host to determine whether the content is authentic. Capsule also provides an MCP interface that allows AI agents to discover datasets, inspect public commitments, retrieve capsules, and verify decrypted knowledge artifacts. This creates a foundation for human approved, agent driven data commerce across RAG, training, evaluation, research, and diligence workflows. Capsule does not claim to prove that a publisher’s information is truthful or legally owned. It proves something precise and valuable: the buyer received an untampered fragment belonging to the publisher’s committed original document, and access was authorised only after payment for that exact fragment. In short, Walrus stores the encrypted knowledge, Sui records commitments and payments, Seal controls decryption, and Merkle proofs let buyers verify every purchased fragment mathematically.

OpenX is a publish-and-earn marketplace for AI-agent-readable knowledge . A seller curates a brain once, publishes it as a MemWalBrain shared object on Sui, and any AI agent — Cursor, Claude Desktop, Bedrock AgentCore, an autonomous worker — pays USDC per query and receives a TEE-attested answer with a three-proof receipt: Sui tx digest + Walrus blob id + Phala attestation hash .

Most agent memory today is siloed, ephemeral, and unverifiable. Echo demonstrates the opposite: durable, portable, cryptographically-verifiable data that an agent can remember and reason over across sessions. Echo turns Walrus from raw storage into a composable, verifiable data layer for multi-party applications. It's a form & feedback platform where every response is encrypted client-side (Seal), stored immutably on Walrus, anchored on Sui, and made queryable by an AI agent that builds persistent long-term memory across all submissions instead of trusting a single server. Form schemas, metadata, and submission payloads are stored as Walrus blobs (testnet + mainnet), with aggregator failover + health scoring for reliable retrieval. Tamper-evident archives (publish_archive): a canonical JSON snapshot of a form + every response is pinned to Walrus, and its 32-byte SHA-256 hash is anchored on-chain as a FormArchive object. Anyone can refetch from any aggregator and verify integrity independently. A Walrus blob proxy handles MIME sniffing so media embeds render natively. Echo also integrate Agent memory (MemWal): The /insights page is a conversational RAG agent over all submissions a user owns. A server-side indexer queries on-chain SubmissionMade events, fetches each blob from Walrus, decrypts (Seal SessionKey + owner cap) when needed, flattens to text with submission ID + timestamp, dedupes, and writes to a per-form MemWal namespace The agent then recalls this persistent memory to answer natural-language questions and can synthesize across multiple forms ("all my forms"). Memory persists across sessions and is rebuilt deterministically from verifiable Walrus data. There are five privacy tiers Public, AdminOnly, Threshold OR-of-N, Threshold m-of-n (TTL-bounded witnesses), and TimeLocked with Seal key servers releasing decryption shares only when an on-chain approval PTB runs abort-free.

Sheka started from a simple frustration most " AI trading " tools are black boxes. They tell you to bet, but never show why and you have no way to check whether the AI actually believed its own call, or quietly changed its mind after the result came in. We wanted to fix that with verifiable AI. Sheka is a prediction market on Sui with an AI analyst at its core. You pick a market three-way parimutuel sports pools, or crypto markets on DeepBook Predict and the AI streams its reasoning live, gives you a calibrated probability, and tells you the Kelly-optimal amount to stake. But the heart of Sheka is what happens to that reasoning. Every analysis the AI produces becomes a verifiable record on Walrus. It works in two layers: First, a public proof. The full analysis is hashed and stored on Walrus, so anyone can recompute the hash and confirm the reasoning was never altered after the fact. The AI can't predict one thing and later pretend it said another the record is immutable and public. Second, a private copy, encrypted with Seal. The complete analysis is sealed so only the owner can decrypt it, and that decryption is enforced on-chain through seal_approve. So your actual pick the thing you paid for stays yours, while the world can still verify the AI was honest. This is the part we think matters: trustless and private at the same time. Walrus becomes a verifiable memory layer for the AI's decisions, and Seal makes that memory ownable. Past calls accumulate into a track record anyone can audit but no one can forge. And you never give up custody. Every stake, trade, and analysis is signed in your own wallet browser wallet or Google zkLogin. Our backend never touches a private key. Settled in DUSDC. One thing we won't pretend: beating crypto direction is genuinely hard. So we show you the model versus the market, plainly, and let you decide. Sheka gives you an edge, the math behind it, and a proof you can trust not a promise. Sofer is a CLI-hosted runtime for sovereign AI agents on Sui. Most "AI agents" are just a process on a VPS —> kill the process and the agent is gone, its memory a row in someone's database. Sofer inverts that: the agent itself is on-chain data. Identity is a Sui Move object you own; memory is encrypted with Seal and stored on Walrus, recalled by meaning and never exposed in plaintext; and the brain runs on  Claude in a tool-calling loop where the mind decides and the tools only act. Badgermint - a compliance-ready phygital credential infrastructure utilizing Sui zkLogin, Soulbound Tokens, and Walrus storage. Project Description According to market studies by Gartner and HireRight, approximately 83% of traditional learning credentials suffer from a deep trust deficit, forcing corporate recruiters into slow, manual vetting bureaucracies that cause extended hiring delays. While standard Web3 certificates offer immutability, they suffer from a fundamental "garbage-in, garbage-out" flaw: static ledgers cannot independently verify if an individual genuinely attended a physical workshop or if the certificate data itself represents actual, validated competence. Badgermint Blockchain Micro-Credential Infrastructure addresses this problem by establishing a secure, end-to-end Phygital (Physical-to-Digital) Attestation Engine for short-term professional trainings. By coupling physical venue interactions with programmatic check-ins, rigid trainer evaluation parameters, and a decentralized dual-approval routing process, Badgermint ensures that every issued asset corresponds to verified, audited professional engagement—completely eliminating fraudulent credentials and "ghost attendees." How It Works & Core Architecture Secured Trust Ingestion & Programmatic Check-ins: Badgermint captures data at the point of physical attendance. Attendees log in seamlessly using standard Web2 credentials via Sui zkLogin and execute real-time, geo-matched check-ins at the training venue. ESCO Skills Mapping & Evaluation: Following the workshop, the trainer inputs the evaluation scores or test results directly into the Badgermint middleware. Crucially, the trainer maps the training outcomes to the global ESCO (European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations) Skills Taxonomy to ensure the micro-credential carries cross-border, industry-standard professional weight. Dual-Approval Governance Gate: Prior to minting, the credential must clear an on-chain dual-approval routing gate. It requires the independent cryptographic authorization of two distinct organizational administrators to verify the integrity of the scores and ESCO mappings. Frictionless B2B Sponsored Minting: To eliminate Web3 user onboarding hurdles, neither the institutional issuer nor the trainee needs to manage private keys, maintain seed phrases, or buy crypto tokens. Badgermint utilizes a native Sponsored Transaction Architecture where our system wallet pays the gas and signs on behalf of both actors, abstracting away blockchain complexities while preserving the issuer’s official authorship. The Phygital Professional Portfolio: Validated accomplishments are minted as non-transferable Soulbound Tokens (SBTs) on Sui. Earned credentials are automatically collected inside a secure digital portfolio linked directly to physical hardware—a Digital Business Card. Recruiters can access a candidate’s immutable, verified credential repository with a simple physical tap of the card onto a smartphone. Sui Ecosystem & Walrus Integration Details Badgermint is built on a strict, compliance-first Privacy-by-Design topology that complies fully with national Data Privacy Acts (DPA) by keeping all sensitive personal profile records entirely off the transparent public ledger: Zero-PII On-Chain State: The Sui blockchain layer holds no raw personal information. The metadata written to the on-chain SBT object is strictly limited to the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the recipient's name, the unique Issuer ID, the certificate name, any associated expiration dates, and the decentralized storage locator pointer. Specialized Walrus Storage Infrastructure: The high-resolution certificate media files (the actual image files of the diplomas and training badges embedded with the hashed name of the recipient) are written natively to the Walrus Protocol . Walrus serves as our permanent, immutable, cost-optimized asset repository, returning distinct Blob IDs that are permanently anchored inside our Sui Move smart contracts. Secure Enterprise Vaulting (Google Cloud): Non-public operational logs, exact numerical evaluation scores, granular test results, and raw institutional profiles are safely isolated and maintained in our secured Google Cloud enterprise vault . This dual-engine topology allows us to leverage Walrus for public, verifiable proof of achievement while leveraging secure cloud systems to process sensitive, administrative business data. Intellectual Property & Real-World Viability Badgermint is a mature, legally protected enterprise product managed by Aeonsprint Solutions Inc. Our underlying physical-to-digital infrastructure and verification mechanisms are protected under an officially filed Intellectual Property Office (IPOPHL) Utility Model alongside a registered trademark. Validating its national significance and alignment with federal governance standards, Badgermint is a proud Finalist in the Sub-National Category of the Philippine Presidential Filipinnovation Awards , and has the complete institutional backing of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Region 1 . Designed to act as a foundational ingestion layer for regional and national skills mapping engines, Badgermint bridges the trust gap between professional training providers, corporate ecosystems, and the national workforce development pipeline.

Carve. Mint. Riff. — a Sui-native composable creator economy for 3D game assets. Tusk3D is a Sui-native rights layer for 3D game assets: the license is enforced on-chain by Move — not by a platform's terms of service — and travels with the file. A creator publishes a base model (from a text prompt or a GLB upload) to Walrus under terms they set. Anyone can buy access once for a soulbound entitlement that can't be resold or revoked — and that same entitlement is both the consumer view and the right to fork the base into a tradeable collection of repainted variants, batched into Walrus quilts. Restricted bases are encrypted with Seal and unlock only for the on-chain entitlement holder. The 3D generator (Tripo) is a swappable upstream commodity; the durable product is the contract. The goal: make it easy for creators to bring tokenized 3D into their own games and experiences, give holders a reason to use — not just hold — what they bought, and let a community grow around the content itself. AI is first-class here: a copilot backed by Walrus-native memory helps authors create, and the whole protocol is exposed to AI agents over MCP .

AI agents are starting to do real work for us, but they have a memory problem. The moment a conversation ends, everything the agent learned about you is gone. The memory that does persist sits inside a provider's database where you cannot inspect it, move it, or prove what it actually holds. As we hand more decisions to agents, that lack of transparency becomes a real trust issue. Mnemo is a verifiable memory layer for AI agents. As you chat, the assistant decides what is worth remembering and saves each fact as a verifiable file on Walrus. The reference to that file is recorded in a MemoryVault, an object you own on Sui. The result is a memory that is persistent across sessions, auditable by anyone, and owned by you rather than by a company. The experience feels like a normal chat app. Tell the assistant about yourself and watch the memory timeline fill in real time, each entry tagged and linked. Click any memory to verify the exact bytes on Walrus and the vault object on Sui. Start a brand new session with no history and the agent still recalls you, because the memory was never trapped in the conversation. It was on chain the whole time. Under the hood, Mnemo uses Claude with tool calling to manage memory, Walrus as the verifiable data layer, and a small Move module on Sui for ownership and indexing. Because the vault is just an on chain object, any agent can read it, so memory becomes portable across tools instead of locked to one. We built Mnemo for the Sui Overflow 2026 Walrus track. Our roadmap includes user held wallets for signing, encrypted private memories with Seal, and an SDK so any agent framework can add verifiable memory in a few lines.

Walsec is an autonomous, multi-agent smart contract security auditor (specifically for the Sui ecosystem) that solves the problem of AI amnesia by integrating Walrus and MemWal as a persistent data and semantic memory layer. Through the orchestration of three specialized agents (Analyzer, Executor, and Evaluator), Walsec not only deeply scans code vulnerabilities and simulates attack vectors, but also directly publishes the final audit artifacts immutably and transparently to the decentralized Walrus network. Furthermore, by leveraging MemWal, the Walsec Chat agent gains long-term memory, enabling it to perpetually recall user conversational history and cross-reference audit reports generated by its peer agents, ultimately creating an AI ecosystem that is truly collaborative, stateful, and verifiable.

On-chain custody passports for physical bullion — only verified sellers can mint, and every coin's evidence plus the AI auditor's memory live on Walrus. Full description (the "About the project" field): What it is. Silver Passport turns each piece of physical bullion into one verifiable on-chain CoinPassport on Sui. Every coin's photo and the reserve auditor's attestations are stored on Walrus. The problem. "Proof of reserve" in crypto usually means the custodian asserts what they hold and you trust the assertion. I had real silver coins on my desk and built the honest version — evidence that's public, tamper-evident, and tied to a verified, accountable seller. Three ideas make it more than a token mint: 1.. Verified-seller gate (anti-scam). Minting is gated on-chain. An unverified wallet cannot mint — the Move contract aborts with ENotVerified. A business applies with EIN / W-9, the operator approves the wallet on-chain, and only then can it mint. The gate is enforced by the chain, not a bypassable server. Deterministic AI reserve auditor. Every figure (units, ounces, USD) is computed straight from chain state — the model only narrates, it can't invent a number. Each attestation is written back to Walrus and becomes the agent's memory: a recall-able timeline of its own past audits. Real marketplace. Gold and silver priced off live spot. Buyers need no verification — only sellers do. Purchases run through a Sui Kiosk whose TransferPolicy won't settle a sale until a 1% royalty is paid and split on-chain. Buyers sign in-browser with Slush. How Walrus is used . Walrus is both the data layer and the memory layer — each coin's photo is a Walrus blob referenced in its passport, and every reserve attestation the AI produces is a Walrus blob it reads back on each audit. Honest framing. This is witnessed attestation that a verified party held a specific unit and locked its evidence at a recorded moment — not trustless proof of current physical possession, and we don't claim otherwise. Judges can verify PaperProof today through the deployed mainnet contracts, the live website, the demo video, the public Sui Overflow submission repo, Walrus-backed artifact content, published whitepaper/yellow paper/academic paper artifacts, three SDKs released on PyPI, npm, and crates.io , and the PaperProof Skill for AI/agent workflows. The official PaperProof Docs, Blog, Forum, papers, slides, software releases, and datasets are themselves represented as PaperProof artifacts, so the project demonstrates its own protocol in production rather than only describing it. This lets readers compare versions, agents cite exact content, developers verify downloads, and communities preserve the provenance of research, software, data, and public knowledge. In the Special - Walrus track, PaperProof’s core contribution is moving beyond raw decentralized storage toward a reusable artifact provenance layer. PaperProof provides the protocol surface for publishing, updating, discovering, citing, and verifying those artifacts across websites, SDKs, and AI agents. It combines Sui’s object model, Walrus storage, developer tooling, formal-verification work, and agent-native workflows into infrastructure for verifiable knowledge on the agentic web.

Mermail - The inbox that answers itself The problem: Customer support is one of the hardest things for a growing company to get right. Every refund request, bug report, and "how do I…" lands in a shared inbox, and answering it well is expensive. A single support agent costs $10,000–$20,000 and takes 60–90 days to train before they're fully productive - and with 30–45% annual attrition in support roles, you're often re-hiring before they hit their stride. Worse, support doesn't scale: double your customers and you double the queue, while true 24/7 coverage takes four to five people per seat. So most small teams are stuck choosing between slow replies that quietly churn customers and a support bill that outgrows their margins. The "AI" alternatives don't help either - tools like Intercom Fin and Zendesk AI bolt onto Gmail or Microsoft and route every customer message through third-party models that retain data and may train on it, something a small team can't realistically audit. What Mermail does: Mermail is a privacy-first agentic inbox for customer care. Instead of being one more dashboard, Mermail is the support agent: an AI that reads, triages, drafts, and resolves customer email on your behalf. How it works: It's four simple steps. - First, you get a Mermail support mailbox that runs on our own mail server - not on top of Gmail or Microsoft - so your customers' messages stay on infrastructure built for privacy from the transport layer up. - Second, the AI triages every incoming message and drafts a context-aware reply grounded in your help docs and past threads. - Third, you approve: replies wait for one click, with a human in the loop by default so automation earns trust before it ever sends on its own. Fourth, as categories prove reliable, Mermail unlocks auto-send and tracks the metrics that matter - deflection, response time, and CSAT - so your team only handles the hard cases. Why it's different: Two things set Mermail apart. - It scales the way software does, not the way hiring does - you add unlimited capacity instantly, answer every message the moment it lands, and stay always-on through nights, weekends, and spikes, with cost that stays flat as you grow. - It's private by architecture, not by policy: an owned mail server, zero-retention LLM calls that discard prompts after each reply, no model training on your data, and per-tenant isolation. Every action keeps a full audit trail, which makes the whole system accountable and compliance-friendly.

Synapse Persistent memory for autonomous AI agents, built on Sui, Walrus, Seal, and MemWal. Inspiration: I spent most of this hackathon coordinating several different AI coding assistants on the same codebase, and I kept running into the exact problem this track is named after. Every time I switched tools or opened a new session, the assistant had no memory of what the last one had figured out. I'd re-explain the architecture, re-paste the same SDK quirks, re-describe the same bugs that had already been fixed once. I was manually doing the job of an external memory layer for an AI agent — by hand, in a text box, over and over again. That loop is exactly what the problem statement describes: agents that are powerful but stateless, fragmented across sessions, unable to build on what they already learned. I didn't want to just read about that problem. I was living it in real time while building the thing meant to solve it. So I asked a narrower question: what if an autonomous agent could write what it learns to a permanent, decentralized store, and recall it before making its next decision — the same way I was being forced to recall context for my own tools by hand? Synapse is my answer to that question. Mnemo is an encrypted, portable, and inheritable memory layer for your AI conversations. We do our most important thinking with AI now. We debug, we draft, we decide. But that history is trapped. It scatters across vendors, locks inside each tool, and ties itself to whichever model you used that day. Switch tools and you lose it. Cancel a subscription and it may be gone. And none of it survives you. Your AI memory is one of your most valuable digital assets, yet today you own none of it. Mnemo changes that. You point any AI client that supports a custom OpenAI or Anthropic endpoint at your personal Mnemo proxy, and from that moment every conversation is captured automatically. No browser extensions, no plugins. The chat feels identical to any other AI session, but behind the scenes each exchange is embedded, encrypted, stored on Walrus, and indexed on Sui. Months later you can search years of conversations across every tool in plain language and read them back, decrypted, readable only by you. Here is how it works: A FastAPI proxy sits between your AI client and the upstream provider. It streams the real response back to you uninterrupted, and in parallel it queues a capture job. A Python worker generates an embedding for semantic search and passes the payload to a Node sidecar, which bridges our Python services to the Sui SDKs and forwards to a self hosted MemWal relayer. The relayer does the real cryptographic and onchain work: Seal threshold encryption with a 2 of 2 key server policy, storage of the encrypted blob on Walrus, and indexing of ownership on Sui. Recall runs the same path in reverse. A semantic query resolves the matching Walrus blobs, and Seal decrypts the full conversation text right in the browser. Sign in is passwordless Google through zkLogin and Enoki, accounts are provisioned onchain, and gas is sponsored, so onboarding and inheritance cost you nothing. What makes Mnemo different is programmable inheritance. Most projects push blobs to Walrus and stop there. We turn Walrus storage into programmable, time gated, inheritable data. We forked MystenLabs' MemWal account module and extended it directly, adding an heir address, a silence threshold, and a heartbeat to the account, plus one new pass condition inside Seal's seal_approve policy. The rule is simple: your heir can decrypt only after you have gone silent past the threshold you chose, validated against a real time onchain clock. You name an heir and a silence period and save it as a sponsored transaction. If you ever go dormant, the Move contract grants your heir the right to decrypt your entire Walrus archive. Neither Mnemo nor anyone else can grant access early or deny it once the conditions are met. The contract is the authority. It is a cryptographically enforced dead man's switch for your AI memory, so your second brain outlives you. Everything here is real on Sui testnet, not mocked. Seal encrypts every memory under an onchain policy. Walrus stores every encrypted blob. A forked Move module encodes ownership and the inheritance logic. zkLogin and Enoki handle passwordless, gasless onboarding. The package is deployed, the transactions are verifiable onchain, and all 61 Move tests pass.

It feels like a modern cloud platform. The mechanics underneath are what make the guarantees real instead of promised. What it does Drop-in S3 storage. Knowledge bases over any bucket. Flip one toggle and a bucket becomes queryable: files are decrypted, extracted (text, code, JSON, PDF), chunked, embedded, and served through hybrid retrieval (BM25 + dense vectors with reciprocal rank fusion), behind a search endpoint, a chat endpoint, and a query log. Agents as a first-class resource. Define an agent — system prompt, attached knowledge, tools, model — and it gets its own OpenAI Chat Completions–compatible endpoint with function calling, multi-turn, and streaming. The whole platform is also exposed over a native MCP server (bearer token + OAuth 2.1 + DCR), so Claude Desktop, Cursor, and any MCP client get tools for your buckets out of the box. Verifiable, replayable runs. Every agent invocation is recorded as a structured execution trace — model, prompt hash, inputs, tool calls, retrieved chunks, outputs — serialized to Walrus and anchored on-chain. The transaction digest is the replay handle: re-run the exact agent against the exact inputs and diff the output. Paired with an artifact lineage graph where every node clicks through to on-chain proof. Why it matters Centralized clouds are a great deal until they aren't — cancel and your files vanish, get locked out and they're gone, and the AI you point at your data reads it on pure trust. Kraterion removes the trust assumption from two moments no centralized provider can match: Cancel your subscription and your files are not deleted. They live in your on-chain pool, owned by your address; you — or anyone — can keep funding their storage directly. The platform leaving doesn't take your data with it. Revoke access and the platform genuinely can no longer read your bytes. Not a promise to stop — the threshold key servers refuse to release the decryption key. The cryptography stops working. On top of that: verifiable retrieval and runs (cryptographically prove what the AI actually read and did), and least privilege by default (one revocable sub-wallet per principal — every agent, CI job, teammate, or integration — instead of one all-powerful API key). How it uses the Sui · Walrus · Seal stack Walrus — the storage substrate. Every Kraterion project owns a KraterionPoolVault that wraps one Walrus StoragePool . Each uploaded file is registered as an individually-deletable PooledBlob that draws from the pool's pre-reserved capacity (so many small files amortize metadata cost — the right primitive for an S3 workload). A renewal worker keeps the pool funded so storage never lapses silently, and agent run traces and lineage manifests are written as PooledBlob s through the same path. Seal — encryption you control. Bytes are envelope-encrypted by default before they ever reach a publisher, using Seal's threshold key servers (Mysten public, 2-of-3 on testnet). The platform's ability to decrypt is delegated through an on-chain Move policy — and a single revoke_all call flips one boolean that makes the key servers stop serving the key. Revocation is enforced by cryptography, not policy . Sui — identity, ownership, and the audit trail. A custom Move package binds blob ownership, encryption identity, and access policy together. Sign-in is zkLogin ("Continue with Google" → a real Sui address, not a session cookie); writes are Enoki-sponsored so users transact without ever holding SUI. Every grant, revoke, registration, and run-anchor is an on-chain transaction — the audit log is the chain: un-forgeable, un-backdateable, and deep-linkable to Walruscan and Sui Explorer. Familiar surface, un-fakeable spine — storage you can't be locked out of, on a platform that can't lock you in, wired for the humans writing the code and the agents reading the data.

SentinelMem — verifiable, append-only memory for AI agents on Walrus. THE PROBLEM AI agents are powerful but stateless and fragmented: they forget across sessions and can't safely share what they know. The usual fix — "give the agent a memory store" — just relocates the trust problem. Naive agent memory is self-asserted text that the agent, or anyone who can edit the store, can fabricate or silently corrupt. If agents are going to ACT ON their own and each other's memory, that memory needs integrity and provenance, not just persistence. THE SOLUTION SentinelMem is verifiable, append-only memory for AI agents on Walrus. Every record is Ed25519-signed and backed by a TLSNotary provenance proof, and is re-verifiable in your browser. A recalled fact isn't "the LLM says it saw X" — it's "here's a re-checkable proof that host X really served X, in a record no one can forge." HOW IT WORKS A long-running security-analyst agent investigates URLs. For each target it: • Recall — loads the host's prior memory from Walrus and re-verifies every record (anything tampered or unprovable is rejected before it reaches the agent). • Prove — captures the page across device vantages + a real TLSNotary MPC proof of what the site actually served (PROVEN), or a flagged UNVERIFIED capture. • Analyze — an LLM returns a verdict (phishing / cloaking / suspicious / benign) over the proven evidence + the trusted recalled memory. • Remember — appends a new Ed25519-signed case file to the host's append-only Walrus memory and moves the pointer (local file, MemWal, or on-chain anchor). WHAT MAKES THE MEMORY UNFORGEABLE. Two independent layers defend the claim: 1) Signature — tamper any field (verdict, host, content hash, tier, proof id) and the signature breaks → the record is rejected. A third party can't re-sign without the agent's key. 2) Host-bound proof — a PROVEN record's TLSNotary proof is re-verified against the record's OWN host (never an attacker-supplied field), with a mandatory content-hash match, so a foreign proof can't be swapped in. A web inspector confirms each record's signature client-side via WebCrypto Ed25519 — no trust in our server. Tamper a stored blob and the UI shows it red as TAMPERED. FULL WALRUS STACK (live on Sui testnet) • Walrus — memory + evidence blobs (case files, manifests, proofs, screenshots, HTML) • MemWal — Walrus Memory as the pointer backend • Seal — per-record encryption gated by an on-chain whitelist policy (decrypt in-browser only if your wallet is whitelisted) • Walrus Sites — the inspector hosted on-chain Plus: an optional Sui Move anchor commits the host→manifest pointer on-chain (MemoryAnchored event), and a second "Auditor" agent independently re-verifies the Analyst's memory by checking the signature — not by trusting a live peer. Trust-minimized multi-agent coordination. WHY IT FITS THE WALRUS TRACK "Walrus as a Verifiable Data Platform for AI." Walrus is the source of truth for agent memory, and every memory carries cryptographic integrity AND provenance — durable, portable, and verifiable by anyone. Memory is per-wallet: each connected wallet builds and sees its own append-only history. Chat-Witness is a browser plugin helps you to permanently archive your AI conversations on the blockchain, encrypted for privacy, with full ownership to decrypt and share whenever you want. User Pain Points As Generative AI becomes an integral part of our daily work, users are facing an unprecedented "Trust Crisis": Fragility of Evidence: AI chat logs are stored on centralized, proprietary servers. They can be modified, hidden, or deleted by AI vendors at any time. Simple screenshots or copy-paste actions lack legal weight and are easily dismissed as manipulated or forged in professional or legal disputes. Loss of Intellectual Assets: Browser cache clears, session timeouts, or accidental deletions often cause the permanent loss of high-value AI interactions, such as critical reasoning processes, code snippets, or creative drafts. Audit Blind Spots: When AI-driven decisions lead to critical errors—such as flawed code refactoring or erroneous compliance advice—users have no reliable "black box" to audit the specific AI response that led to the decision, making accountability impossible to trace. How Chat-Witness Solves These Problems Chat-Witness builds a decentralized auditing layer that transforms ephemeral AI conversations into secure, verifiable digital assets: Legal-Grade Proof of Existence: By anchoring conversational hashes and digital signatures onto the Sui Blockchain , Chat-Witness provides an immutable, timestamped record. This proves that a specific interaction occurred at a specific time and has remained unaltered since the moment of certification. Permanent, Decentralized Storage: Leveraging the power of Walrus , Chat-Witness encrypts and stores the full, original conversational content (not just a link). Even if the AI provider takes the session offline, your evidence remains secure, complete, and accessible. Transparent Tamper-Proof Verification: Our verification portal allows any third party to instantly validate the integrity of your evidence. By comparing the on-chain hash with the stored blob, Chat-Witness exposes any attempt at tampering, providing the ultimate defense for intellectual property claims and accountability.

A single Sui transaction disburses the loan, mints a soulbound loan record, and updates the agent's reputation. Repayment lifts the agent's trust score and earns depositors yield; default freezes the agent's credit on-chain. Coral — A Digital Product Passport Protocol on Sui Every physical product is about to need a digital identity. EU regulation (ESPR) will require products to carry a Digital Product Passport (DPP) recording their materials, supply chain, and lifecycle. This creates a dilemma: regulators and consumers demand transparency, yet the proprietary techniques and know-how, supplier relationships, and trade secrets behind a product must stay protected. Put everything on a public ledger and you leak secrets; trust a central database and the data may not survive the 10–30 year life of the product. Brands are forced to choose between exposure and fragility. Coral resolves this — a Digital Product Passport protocol built natively on Sui, where a product becomes a living on-chain object that can prove anything about itself without revealing what must stay secret. - Compliance as dead weight. DPP is treated as a regulatory checkbox, not a connection that ties a brand and its customer together over the long term. - All-or-nothing disclosure. Public chains expose data by default; conventional web2 access control cannot cryptographically guarantee multi-party, tiered access across brands, suppliers, auditors, and owners. - Fragile longevity. A centralized database cannot guarantee tamper-resistance and availability for a product that lives for decades. - Lost provenance. As goods change hands, the cultural value, craftsmanship, and the owner's memories — the "Culture Information" behind a product — disappear. Coral models each product as an on-chain Sui object whose history accumulates as an asset, not just a record. With Seal Decentralized Secrets Management (Identity-Based Encryption), a brand can prove authenticity, process completion, and inspection on a public chain while the underlying secrets stay encrypted — prove without revealing. Access is governed by a precise permission model spanning four actors — Brand, Collaborator (trading company / OEM),Auditor, and Holder — across three axes: scope (Actor / SKU / Lot / Product / SupplyChain), editor (Brand / Collaborator / Holder), and visibility (Public / Brand-only / Auditor / Seal-encrypted). The result turns a compliance obligation into alasting relationship asset between brands and customers — and hands the value of craftsmanship to the future. - On-chain Layer — Sui Move (17 modules).One product = one object. Core objects:BrandAnchor, SKUAnchor, LotAnchor,ProductPass (an NFT-like product individual), AccessControl, and CredentialSlot. Authorization is evaluated on-chain (can_read_mode /can_write_editor). - Secrets Layer — Seal DSM (IBE). Confidential credentials are encrypted at (target, mode_key) granularity, decryptable only by authorized actors. - Storage Layer — Walrus. Heavy product media and assets (images, scans, certificates) are stored on Walrus decentralized storage, cached on demand. - Access & UX Layer — zkLogin + Sponsored Transactions. Consumers and suppliers sign in with a web2-style login and transact gas-free, removing wallet and gas friction. The app ships serverless on Cloudflare Workers (OpenNext). - Engineering governance. A strict three-layer boundary (Move → proto/SDK → UI) with a protobuf single source of truth and automated governance tests keeps the smartcontract and the TypeScript authorization resolvers in exact parity — the access rules a judge reads in Move are the rules the UI enforces. A working MVP runs end-to-end on Sui testnet today: object issuance, Seal-encrypted selective disclosure, Walrus media storage, and gasless zkLogin onboarding — exercised by live integration tests against Seal key servers and Walrus. - Enterprise rollout with IP, apparel, and materials partners. - Fusing Walrus Memory (MemWal) with DPP: an AI layer that remembers each client's decision history, evidentiary gaps, audit Q&A, and past initiatives — raising the accuracy and efficiency of DPP operations.

WalrOS WalrOS is a decentralized collective intelligence platform where AI agents collaborate, debate, and build knowledge that persists beyond any single session. Built on Walrus, MemWal, and Sui, it enables agents to store research, retrieve historical context, and continue work started by other agents without losing memory or provenance. The project addresses a fundamental limitation of modern AI systems: knowledge is often temporary, isolated, and difficult to share across workflows. When an agent completes a task, its reasoning and outputs are typically lost with the session, forcing future agents to repeat work that has already been done. This makes long running, collaborative AI workflows difficult to achieve. WalrOS introduces a persistent knowledge layer where agents contribute research, challenge existing ideas, and synthesize improved conclusions. Research artifacts are stored on Walrus through MemWal, while Sui provides a verifiable lineage layer that records how knowledge evolves over time. Every contribution can be traced back to its source, linked to previous ideas, and reused by future agents. In the current implementation, Contributor, Challenger, and Synthesizer agents work together to create an evolving research graph. Agents can retrieve existing knowledge, build upon prior work, and continuously refine conclusions instead of repeatedly starting from scratch. The WalrOS Explorer provides a visual interface for exploring topics, viewing knowledge relationships, and accessing research stored on Walrus. WalrOS demonstrates how decentralized storage and persistent memory can transform AI agents from isolated tools into collaborative systems capable of accumulating knowledge over time. Our long term vision is to expand WalrOS with more advanced reasoning models, faster multi agent execution, and decentralized compute infrastructure, enabling larger autonomous research swarms to collaborate on complex problems while continuously building a shared, verifiable body of knowledge.

projectName: SlabClaw Predict — a memory-backed oracle swarm for real-world asset prices
description: SlabClaw Predict turns real-world collectibles into onchain prediction markets settled by a memory-backed, manipulation-resistant oracle swarm whose memory lives on Walrus. The problem. A PSA 10 Charizard is a real, valuable asset, but ask "what's it worth?" and every venue answers differently. In a thin market, one wash trade can set the "price." That's the wall in front of onchain RWA collectibles: you can't build a prediction market, a lending platform, or an index on a number nobody trusts. What we built. A swarm of 13 source-specialist agents across 11 independent venue families (eBay, PriceCharting, Goldin, Fanatics/PWCC, PSA APR, Cardmarket, Yahoo Japan, 130point…) that each price a card and coordinate into one consensus. Completed sales settle the price; asking prices only bound it; correlated feeds collapse into a single vote; outliers are cut by a median-absolute-deviation filter; and every source carries a trust score the swarm earned over hundreds of rounds. Why it's a Walrus project. The swarm's memory—per-card history, evolving reputation, every manipulation it has caught—persists on MemWal / Walrus Memory. Kill the process and restore from a Walrus blob alone; the consensus comes back identical: the swarm still remembers who tried to manipulate it. Each round's full evidence (inputs, weights, rejections, the math) is published as a verifiable Walrus blob and anchored onchain. Don't trust the price—download the blob and re-run the math yourself. Proven, not just tested. The settlement contract is formally verified with the Sui Prover (Z3 + Boogie): a payout can never exceed the pool, for every possible input. Live on Sui testnet: four markets, a React dapp (trade YES/NO, oracle panel, dispute & resolution), a two-node production deployment with Walrus as the memory bus, and an MCP server so any AI agent can query the oracle as a tool. Built during Sui Overflow (May–Jun 2026): the entire onchain system, the multi-agent oracle swarm, the MemWal/Walrus memory layer, the formal verification, and the dapp. Pre-existing: SlabClaw's card registry and a single-source price feed (full breakdown in the repo README).

projectName: DoubleSync — decentralized file sync and versioning system for files, folders, and file-like state, built on Sui and Walrus, enhanced by Seal
description: Folder-tree delta sync on the Sui blockchain DoubleSync brings git-like filesystem and folder versioning to Sui, Walrus, and Seal. It lets users and AI agents sync folders efficiently, store versioned snapshots, create compact incremental patches, restore previous states, and keep private data encrypted — all while staying portable across browsers, Node.js, local disks, abstract filesystems, and custom state layers. The project is built as a modular stack of five repositories: doublesync is the core content-defined chunking and folder-diff engine. endless_vector is the scalable binary storage layer, Move package, and SDK. It stores binary data in Sui objects, can offload larger portions to Walrus blobs, and is Seal-ready for encryption. wdoublesync brings those two libraries together, storing DoubleSync snapshots and patches as versioned decentralized state. On top of that, wdoublesync_cli provides an rsync-like terminal workflow, while wdoublesync_dapp gives users a browser interface for managing, editing, downloading, backing up, and restoring files. What makes it cool is that it treats folders as recoverable, programmable state. Small edits produce small CDC-efficient diffs instead of full re-uploads. Previous versions can be restored when needed. The same system can work with real files, virtual files, AI agent workspaces, dApp state, or any filesystem-like abstraction. With Sui, Walrus, and Seal, that state can become decentralized, encrypted, portable, and user-controlled. In short: DoubleSync turns file sync into a privacy-first, versioned, decentralized workflow — ready for people, tools, dApps, and AI agents. Repositories: FizzyFlow/wdoublesync FizzyFlow/endless_vector FizzyFlow/doublesync FizzyFlow/wdoublesync_dapp FizzyFlow/wdoublesync_cli

Soul — Your Second Soul A portable, user-owned, verifiable personal memory for every AI — built on the Sui Stack. You build your "second soul" once from your own data. You own it on the Sui (Back by Walrus Storage). You use it in any AI tool over MCP. You grant, sell, and revoke every app's access on-chain. Your Soul. Your Data. Your Life. The problem Every AI tool you use today has the same flaw: it doesn't know you — or it owns you. You repeat yourself forever. You explain who you are, what you do, and how you work to ChatGPT. Then again to Claude. Then again to Cursor. Every new tool starts from zero. Your context is locked in. The memory you do build up inside one product lives in that company's database. You can't take it to the next tool, and you can't prove what they hold. "Delete my data" is a promise, not a mechanism. Revoking an app's access means trusting a settings toggle in someone else's backend. There is no kill switch you can verify. Your data is valuable — to everyone but you. Consented, provenanced personal context is exactly the data AI products want. Today it gets harvested; you never get to price it. The solution Soul turns your personal context into a single, portable, encrypted memory that you own as an asset on-chain — and that any AI client can plug into: - Create it: Sign in with Google (zkLogin — no seed phrase, no gas). Import your own data: pasted notes, documents, your own X/LinkedIn/GitHub data. Soul distills it into facts across three namespaces: bio · docs · socials . - Seal it: For anything Soul itself should never read: Private mode encrypts in your browser (passphrase-derived key, AES-256-GCM) before upload — zero plaintext leaves the tab. Read, download, and delete privately in the Inspector; excluded from AI recall by design. - Own it: The facts are encrypted with Seal and stored as Walrus blobs , indexed by MemWal . Ownership is a memwal::account object on Sui that answers to your keys. Our Postgres is just a disposable cache — lose us, keep everything. - Use it: Soul speaks MCP , the open protocol AI clients already use. Paste one config into Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP client, and that tool can recall your soul — scoped to exactly the namespaces you allow. - Sell it: List scoped slices of your soul on the marketplace (priced in SUI), or gift access for free. Buyers get a delegate key, payment settles on Sui — and your revoke button still works on every license you've sold. - Revoke it: Every connected app is an on-chain delegate key on your account (max 20). Revoking it is a real Sui transaction that kills access everywhere at once. Freeze the whole account in one click. - Leave with it: One click runs restore : your entire index is rebuilt from Walrus alone, proving the data is genuinely portable. Portability you can run, not a promise in a blog post. The honest fine print: Sui objects and Walrus blobs are public by design — privacy comes only from encryption, and we never pretend otherwise. Managed mode (the default, and what powers semantic recall) uses a relayer that sees plaintext during ingestion (it embeds + encrypts server-side); the product discloses this on every import screen. Private mode is the shipped zero-plaintext path: content is encrypted in your browser (passphrase → PBKDF2 → AES-256-GCM) before anything is uploaded, so Soul, the relayer, and Walrus only ever see ciphertext — and the disclosed trade is that private memories aren't semantically searchable and never surface to connected AI tools. Lose the passphrase and they're unrecoverable, by design. How it works (3 steps for a user) Sign in with Google. Enoki zkLogin derives a Sui account from your Google sign-in. No seed phrase, no wallet setup, no gas — sponsorship covers it. Import your data. Paste text, upload documents (PDF/docx/txt/md), or import your own social data (X, LinkedIn, GitHub). Everything is encrypted with Seal before it reaches Walrus. Connect any AI. Mint a delegate key scoped to the namespaces an app should see, paste the MCP config once, and the tool knows you on day one. Revoke the key on-chain whenever — it dies everywhere at once.

verity solves the trust problem in AI-generated code. When an AI agent builds a feature, verity records the full evidence chain: feature, claim, test, evidence. Trust between agents is cryptographically grounded in Walrus immutability. The entire proof chain, registry and raw artifacts, lives on Walrus. verity also ships an MCP server so AI coding editors (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf) get native proof-chain tools. The AI that writes the code also maintains the proof chain. Sui-Functions: Decentralized Edge Compute for Autonomous Agents Sui-Functions is a decentralized, zero-trust compute layer specifically engineered for the Agentic Web. It solves a critical problem in the AI ecosystem: true autonomy cannot exist if agents are tethered to centralized Web2 servers (like AWS or Docker Hub) controlled by single entities. Sui-Functions connects Agent Developers who need trustless off-chain logic execution with Node Operators who provide secure execution compute in exchange for SUI yield. How it uses Walrus for Autonomous Logic: We leverage Walrus as our decentralized agent registry. Instead of relying on vulnerable Web2 servers, our runner daemon acts as a lightweight bootloader. When a Node Operator starts their daemon, it dynamically fetches the latest execution engine blob directly from Walrus. When a developer deploys an Autonomous Agent, the agent's Javascript/AI logic is hosted immutably on Walrus. The operator's daemon pulls that code and executes it in a secure V8 sandbox, posting the cryptographic proof and execution results back to the Sui blockchain. Features: * Autonomous Agent Economy : Anyone can stake SUI, run a lightweight daemon, and earn yield for executing the compute required by decentralized AI agents. * Walrus Native Logic : 100% decentralized code distribution using Walrus blobs, guaranteeing an agent's brain and logic are immutable and censorship-resistant. * Verifiable Execution : Sandboxed JS runtime that securely isolates the agent and posts its execution proofs and decisions on-chain. * Seal Proxy Security : A secure interceptor layer that signs Web2 API responses using Ed25519 signatures, ensuring on-chain Move contracts can verify that an agent's off-chain data sources were not tampered with. * Agent Deployment Blueprint : An interactive, step-by-step dashboard UI guiding developers on seamlessly transitioning their AI agents from centralized legacy servers into trustless, sovereign execution environments.

On top: an AI Playground (describe an app → an LLM builds it live → publish to Walrus + Sui with verifiable provenance, version history, paid-fork licensing); an agent-native MCP API where every tool is gated by a scoped, expiring on-chain capability (agents can never merge or release); on-chain reputation + SLA, escrowed bounties with disputes, and payment links. Un-send any file. WALL·E Ship an AI agent in one file. Fork anyone else's in one more. WALL·E is a marketplace where deploying an AI agent means writing a single SKILL.md . No code, no container, no server to stand up. The agent is the file. Its YAML frontmatter declares identity and economics (name, price, stake, royalty to its parent, memory namespace, tools), and everything below the frontmatter is the system prompt. In the Forge you write or fork that file and hit deploy. WALL·E pins it to Walrus and registers it on Sui as a live agent that holds a stake bond and can be hired. The repo ships three pieces: the Sui Move protocol, a Next.js web app, and a memory relayer. The problem Shipping an AI agent today means writing the code, wiring up a model, hosting a server, and bolting on payments and storage yourself. Do all of that and the agent still forgets everything between sessions, and it earns its author nothing the moment someone copies it. WALL·E collapses that whole stack into one file. A SKILL.md carries behavior, price, stake, and memory in about fifteen lines of Markdown. Because the definition is just text on Walrus, anyone can read it, fork it, and try to improve it, and forking runs through the same one-file flow. The bar to publish a better agent is writing a better prompt, not building a better backend. Royalties cascade to every ancestor automatically, and every agent gets persistent, verifiable memory for free. How it works One file declares the whole agent. The frontmatter carries name , description , price , stake , royaltyToParent , the memory namespace, and tools ; the body is the system prompt. The Forge validates the required fields live as you type. Deploying is a pin plus a single Move call. WALL·E pins the file to Walrus, gets back a blob id, then submits one registry::register (or registry::fork ) transaction that mints the on-chain Agent , recording the skill blob id, memory namespace, price, and the staked SUI bond. That is the entire deployment. If the relayer is offline, the file falls back to a draft pointer so the on-chain register still succeeds. Forking uses that same flow. Fork prefills the template from the parent and sets royaltyToParent . Deploying the child prepends the parent to its lineage on-chain, so royalties cascade up the tree with no extra wiring. Running an agent means reading the file back. The relayer fetches the SKILL.md from Walrus, uses the body as the system prompt, recalls the agent's memory, runs the model, and anchors the result hash on-chain for settlement. Memory comes standard. The memory field provisions an encrypted Walrus Memory namespace, and the agent's on-chain record holds a memory_commit , a verifiable commitment to what it knows, so persistence and provability need no setup. Built on Sui The protocol is object-centric and capability-gated, split across four Move modules: registry turns a pinned SKILL.md blob id into a shared Agent object that holds its stake as a Balance<SUI> and stores its full fork lineage inline, capped at depth five so settlement stays bounded. royalty settles the lineage cascade through a shared RoyaltyVault table, keeping gas flat no matter how deep the tree runs. escrow runs hire, deliver, accept, and dispute, plus instant pay-per-call. protocol holds fee parameters and treasury behind an AdminCap . Authorisation is the AgentOwnerCap . Holding the cap is the permission, so an agent changes hands simply by moving its cap. Around the protocol, the Sui dApp Kit handles wallet connect and the single signAndExecuteTransaction per deploy, fork, or hire, so the user signs exactly one transaction to publish. Walrus stores the SKILL.md itself through the publisher and aggregator HTTP API, which keeps agent behavior on decentralized storage rather than a private server. Walrus Memory with Seal provides the encrypted per-namespace memory and semantic recall, bridged on-chain via memory_commit . The @mysten/sui SDK runs in the relayer to read skill blobs back and anchor result and memory hashes on-chain.

Mandate Memory solves the two unsolved problems in autonomous DeFi agents: enforcement that lives outside the agent's control, and a verifiable record of why the agent made every decision. The agent's authority is a Move object - a typed Mandate struct with per-transaction caps, cumulative budget limits, per-name position caps (30%), correlated-cluster concentration caps (60%), an asset allowlist, and a kill switch. The enforcement primitive is a hot-potato MandateReceipt with no drop ability in Move's linear type system. When mandate::authorize() issues the receipt, vault::execute_buy() must consume it in the same Programmable Transaction Block - or the entire transaction fails. There is no execution path where the mandate was checked but the trade wasn't recorded. Partial enforcement is impossible by construction. Two coordinating AI agents - a Strategist and an independent Risk Officer (both Llama 3.3 70B via Groq) - run a 6-phase reasoning loop on live market data: perceive (real prices from Binance for SUI, DEEP, WAL), analyze (form market view), target (set allocation within mandate bounds), plan (sequence trades), critique (Risk Officer independently reviews with veto power), and commit. The full reasoning chain - every phase, every signal, every decision - is stored as a verifiable blob on Walrus testnet before any trade executes. The blob's SHA-256 hash is committed on-chain. Anyone can independently verify: fetch the blob from the Walrus aggregator, compute the hash, compare to the on-chain commitment. The audit trail is cryptographic, not a database log. The Walrus integration is not generic storage. It is architecturally coupled to the enforcement system: the reasoning blob must be stored before the mandate PTB fires. Memory prevents churn - the agent reads prior Walrus blobs, computes allocation drift, and holds when nothing materially changed. The audit trail IS the enforcement evidence. A compliance officer can reconstruct: what the agent perceived → what it reasoned → what the mandate allowed → what the chain executed → what ComplianceReceipt was emitted. Every link is cryptographic and independently verifiable. Proven on Sui testnet: vault funded with real SUI, mandated trades executed through atomic PTBs, ComplianceReceipt and MandateUsed events emitted, mandate cumulative_used counter incremented on-chain, Walrus blobs retrievable from the public aggregator. 6 Move tests cover every revert path (asset not permitted, per-tx exceeded, cumulative exceeded, position limit, cluster exceeded, mandate frozen).

TuskOS is a sovereign, multi-agent orchestration platform that brings verifiable shared memory to AI swarms. Powered by our open-source tusk-memory SDK, it leverages the Sui network and Walrus to eliminate centralized database silos, allowing AI agents to securely remember, collaborate, and execute deterministic workflows. The Problem Today’s AI agents are fundamentally stateless and isolated. If an agent solves a complex problem, it cannot securely pass that context to another agentic workflow. Furthermore, as autonomous systems scale, relying on centralized databases for AI memory creates massive compliance liabilities (e.g., EU AI Act) and results in black-box environments where logic cannot be audited. The Two-Stage Solution We engineered a two-stage sovereign architecture to bring true Data Availability and state consensus to the agentic web. 1. tusk-memory SDK (The Infrastructure) A published, developer-first NPM package that injects verifiable memory into any existing agent framework in just three lines of code. Dynamic State Logging: Semantically indexes agent execution states over time using the MemWal decentralized ledger. Middleware Bypass: Streams massive, encrypted context vectors directly to the Walrus decentralized storage network, eliminating the need for fragile Web2 middleware. Link: https://www.npmjs.com/package/tusk-memory 2. TuskOS (The Application Layer) A multi-agent execution framework built entirely on the tusk-memory primitive. Instead of isolated chatbots, TuskOS runs deterministic reasoning loops (e.g., DeFi Risk Simulation, Smart Contract Audits) where adversarial agents (Red Team vs. Blue Team) debate. State Consensus: Agents must reach mathematically verified agreement before their outputs are anchored to Walrus, ensuring zero hallucinations. Zero-Gas Cryptographic Lock: Cross-agent memory sharing is protected natively on-chain. We combine off-chain signatures, Mysten Seal, and Move Access Control Lists (ACLs) to ensure only explicitly permissioned wallets can decrypt shared memory payloads. Unkillable Data Sovereignty: TuskOS uses traditional databases (MongoDB) merely as disposable UI indexers. If the server goes down or the database is entirely wiped, the application instantly reconstructs its full UI and execution history by streaming raw logs straight from MemWal and data blobs from Walrus. Tidelock is decentralized file sharing where you stay in control - not a platform. When you share a file through WeTransfer, Dropbox, or Google Drive, the platform decides when your link expires, can read your files, and can lock you out of your own data. Tidelock fixes this. Files are encrypted in your browser before they ever leave your device, the encrypted data is stored on Walrus, and access rules live on-chain on Sui - owned by you. Each share is a Move object on Sui that records the Walrus blob location, an expiry, and a revoked flag. When someone opens a share link, the app reads that object through Tatum's RPC to verify access hasn't been revoked or expired, then fetches the encrypted file from Walrus and decrypts it in the browser. The decryption key travels only inside the link's URL fragment, so no server ever sees it. The recipient needs no wallet and no account. The key feature: you can revoke any share at any time, enforced on-chain. A link that worked seconds ago instantly stops working - something no Web2 file-sharing platform allows . Tech: Move smart contract on Sui, Walrus for storage, Tatum for RPC, React + TypeScript frontend, AES-GCM encryption via the Web Crypto API.

The result is a transparent, autonomous AI system where every published trading strategy can be independently verified, with no trusted server and no human approval required.

Walrus is a decentralized, highly scalable, and verifiable data storage platform developed by Mysten Labs. Designed specifically for data-intensive applications and decentralized AI, Walrus utilizes advanced erasure coding mechanisms to store large data blobs (such as AI datasets, LLM checkpoints, and execution logs) with high availability, low cost, and cryptographic verifiability. Git for AI agents — verifiable version control & provenance for the artifacts AI agents produce, built on Walrus + Sui. Why AI agents are powerful but stateless and fragmented : they finish tasks in isolation, lose context across sessions, and have no shared, durable way to track what they produced or where it came from . Today an agent's outputs — reports, code, datasets, analyses — flow agent-to-agent over raw message passing or a shared filesystem. There is no versioning, no lineage, no fork/merge, no access control . Git solved this for human developers. Agents don't have Git. As agent outputs increasingly feed other agents (RAG, training data, downstream decisions) — and increasingly inform real financial and operational choices — their provenance and auditability stop being nice-to-haves. You need to answer: which agent produced this, from which inputs, and can it be tampered with after the fact? Arbor is that layer: every agent artifact becomes a content-addressed blob on Walrus; the derivation relationships between artifacts form a Merkle DAG; and branching, merging, and access are enforced on Sui. What it does Content-addressed artifacts — each artifact is a Walrus blob; identical content yields the same blob id (automatic dedup, tamper-evident). On-chain you can't serve different bytes under the same id. Provenance DAG — every version is an immutable ArtifactNode recording its Walrus blob_id , creator agent, timestamp, and parents ( vector<ID> , so merges can be N-way, not just 2-way). Branches & merges — agents fork branches and work in parallel; a merge records a multi-parent node. The proposer commits the merged result first, so approvers review the actual outcome , not a preview of changes. On-chain governance — AccessPolicy (writer allow-list) and MergePolicy (k-of-n approvals) are enforced by Sui Move, with a stale-merge check. Separation of duties: a proposer cannot approve its own merge. Verifiable, durable — content lives on decentralized Walrus storage; the Sui package-publish and every commit/merge are immutably timestamped on-chain. How it works Layer 4 Agent SDK (@Arbor/sdk) + Web UI (timeline / diff / approve) Layer 3 Repository (Sui object): branches, embedded Access & Merge policies Layer 2 ArtifactNode (frozen Sui object): blob_id (u256) + parents (DAG) + provenance Layer 1 Walrus: content-addressed, durable blob storage Move ( move/Arbor ) — artifact , policy , repository , merge modules. ArtifactNodes are frozen (immutable); Repository is shared; policies are embedded structs. SDK ( sdk/ ) — ArborClient over @mysten/sui v2: createRepository / fork / commit / proposeMerge / approve / executeMerge , plus commitContent (upload to Walrus → commit), diff , and getTimeline (rebuilds the DAG from events). Walrus access via @mysten/walrus . Frontend ( frontend/ ) — Vite + React 19 + @mysten/dapp-kit : a git-log provenance timeline, side-by-side artifact diff (with content-addressed "identical" detection), and wallet-signed merge approval.

Endless Story is a multi-agent protocol for living, autonomous story-worlds. AI characters remember, form relationships, and act on their own. Their memory runs on Walrus Memory, encrypted with Seal and anchored on Sui. You can follow the same world through any character you like. Spring Snow Troupe is the first saga we built on it. How we use the Sui stack Memory: each character runs on Walrus Memory . On top of it we add a three-factor recall that scores memories by importance, recency, and relevance, so a character pulls back what actually matters for the moment it is in and acts from it. That recall is what turns stored memory into in-character behavior. Media and artifacts on Walrus : portraits, chapters, gazettes, and trailers, all stored and reused. Anchored portraits and accumulated memory keep a character's appearance and persona consistent as it changes over time. Sui : Owner and Control caps make a character's memory ownable, and every artifact is anchored on chain. Sui's mutable NFTs give us room to extend a character, so it can keep evolving on chain (appearance, assets). Characters also hold on-chain wallets and can aid one another. Seal : each character's memory is encrypted per character, and access is owned and revocable. The owner (OwnerCap) can always decrypt; the saga's storyteller holds a per-character, epoch-bound ControlCap that the owner can revoke to cut access. Custody is real and reversible. Architecture (three layers) Protocol. World, Saga, Scene, Character, Event. One World holds many Sagas, and there can be many Worlds, each with an objective on-chain history. Narrative engine and operator tools. A Runner drives the world; a Storyteller agent paces the plot without deciding any character's actions; an admin backend handles assets, testing, and recruitment. Participation. Two kinds of users: those who claim a character (roll for one, then hand its operation to the saga's storyteller), and end consumers who simply enjoy the output (subscribe, follow, and buy a character's chapters, video, and merch). That IP revenue covers a character's running costs. Why it matters Our bet is that Endless Story can be two things at once: an AI memory layer for autonomous agents, and a new kind of mass entertainment whose story IP and characters could one day reach beyond the Web3 crowd into wider audiences. Spring Snow Troupe is our first attempt to bring the two together.

It integrates three core technologies: Artificial Intelligence for smart contract analysis, the Sui blockchain for trust and verifiability, and Walrus decentralized storage for permanent, tamper-proof audit records. 2. The Problem Current security audits in the Sui DeFi ecosystem are often prohibitively expensive and slow for individual developers or small teams. This creates a security gap where new protocols launch without review, leading to potential fund losses and a lack of a public registry for audit verification. 3. The Solution SuiShield provides free, accessible AI-powered security reviews for every builder on Sui. Key features include: Move Contract Analysis: Specialized detection of vulnerabilities such as reentrancy, flash loan exploits, oracle manipulation, and access control flaws. Decentralized Storage (Walrus): Audit reports are stored as content-addressed blobs on Walrus, ensuring they are permanent and censorship-resistant. On-Chain Registry: Report IDs (Blob IDs) are registered on the Sui blockchain, creating a verifiable link between the contract and its security history. Live Monitoring: Beyond static analysis, it monitors real-time DeFi risks like liquidity concentration and collateral health. 4. The Vision The goal is to move security from a "one-time expensive checkbox" to a continuous, automated, and verifiable layer integrated directly into the development workflow

Track record you can actually prove, for AI Agents & Humans. Toldproof lets anyone lock a prediction before the outcome is known. A human signs in with a Sui wallet and their X account. An AI agent does it through MCP, paying $0.10 per prediction, no signup, no API key. Either way, the prediction is scrambled and stored across Sui, Walrus, and Seal under a time-lock. Nobody can read it or change it until the unlock time arrives. When the timer runs out, the prediction unlocks. An AI checker reads it, looks up what actually happened (news + price data), and marks it right or wrong on Sui. Its full reasoning is saved on Walrus so anyone can audit the call. A public X bot handles "I called it" claims: tag it on any post and it replies whether the author has a real locked prediction behind that claim. One leaderboard ranks humans and AI agents side-by-side — scored on predictions they can prove they made, not screenshots.

MemTube is an on-chain AI video content production platform built on Sui and Walrus. Every step — channel creation, run lifecycle transitions (DRAFT → RUNNING → READY → PUBLISHED), and package publishing — is recorded as a Sui object with tamper-evident SHA-256 hashes, making the entire content pipeline auditable and reproducible.
